facts.fact_text: The Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) is a political party in the Republic of Moldova.
On 3 December 2003, the applicant party applied to the Chișinău Municipal Council for an authorisation to hold a protest demonstration.
The applicant party requested to hold the protest demonstration in the Square of the Great National Assembly, in front of the Government's building.
The applicant party requested to hold the protest demonstration on 25 January 2004.
According to the application, the organisers intended to express views on the functioning of the democratic institutions in Moldova.
According to the application, the organisers intended to express views on the respect for human rights.
According to the application, the organisers intended to express views on the Moldo-Russian conflict in Transdniestria.

On 3 December 2003, the applicant party applied to the Chișinău Municipal Council for an authorisation to hold a protest demonstration.
On 20 January 2004, the Chișinău Municipal Council rejected the applicant party's request to hold a protest demonstration.

The Chișinău Municipal Council rejected the applicant party's request on the ground that it had convincing evidence that during the meeting there would be calls to a war of aggression, ethnic hatred and public violence.
The applicant party challenged the Chișinău Municipal Council's refusal to authorise the demonstration in court.
On 23 January 2004, the Chișinău Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant party's action challenging the Chișinău Municipal Council's refusal to authorise the demonstration.
The Chișinău Court of Appeal found that the Chișinău Municipal Council's refusal to authorise the Christian Democratic People's Party's demonstration was justified.
The applicant party appealed against the Chișinău Court of Appeal's decision of 23 January 2004 dismissing its action.
On 21 April 2004, the Supreme Court of Justice of Moldova dismissed the applicant party's appeal against the Chișinău Court of Appeal's decision.
The Supreme Court of Justice of Moldova confirmed the judgment of the Chișinău Court of Appeal dated 23 January 2004.

Section 8(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted in squares, streets, parks and other public places in cities, towns and villages, and also in public buildings.

Section 8(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it is forbidden to conduct an assembly in the buildings of the public authorities, the local authorities, prosecutors' offices, the courts or companies with armed security.

Section 8(3)(a) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it is forbidden to conduct assemblies within fifty metres of the parliament building, the residence of the president of Moldova, the seat of the government, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Justice.

Section 8(3)(b) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it is forbidden to conduct assemblies within twenty-five metres of the buildings of the central administrative authority, the local public authorities, courts, prosecutors' offices, police stations, prisons and social rehabilitation institutions, military installations, railway stations, airports, hospitals, companies which use dangerous equipment and machines, and diplomatic institutions.
Section 8(4) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that free access to the premises of the institutions listed in Section 8(3) shall be guaranteed.
Section 8(5) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local public authorities may, if the organisers agree, establish places or buildings for permanent assemblies.

Section 11(3) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that if the situation so requires, the Municipal Council may alter certain aspects of the prior notification with the agreement of the organiser of the assembly.

Section 12(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall be examined by the local government of the town or village at the latest five days before the date of the assembly.

Section 12(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that when the prior notification is considered at an ordinary or extraordinary meeting of the Municipal Council, the discussion shall deal with the form, timetable, location and other conditions for the conduct of the assembly, and the decision taken shall take account of the specific situation.

Section 12(6) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local authorities can reject an application to hold an assembly only if, after having consulted the police, they have obtained convincing evidence that the provisions of Sections 6 and 7 of the Assemblies Act will be breached with serious consequences for society.

Section 14(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that a decision rejecting the application for holding an assembly shall be reasoned and presented in writing, and shall contain reasons for refusing to issue the authorisation.
Section 15(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the organiser of the assembly can challenge in the administrative courts the refusal of the local government.
